clauses.reason: Exhausted by performance on February 5, 1960, the date the order was signed. Its only operative words revoke Executive Order No. 10758 of March 4, 1958, which established a career executive program within the civil-service system, and Executive Order No. 10777 of August 6, 1958, which amended it to increase the membership of the Career Executive Board, a one-time act that commands nothing afterwards. The order has no effective-date wording, so it is read as effective when signed; the Federal Register issue of February 9, 1960 is the alternative reading and is disclosed here. Actor: the order itself; the end source is its own operative text. The revoked order's non-operation is the surviving consequence, not a continuing command.

research_rationale:
Identity: the registered original is the Federal Register printing of Executive Order 10859 (25 FR 1089, PDF pages 1-4; Federal Register issue of February 9, 1960; govinfo PDF text layer held at jobs/fr-originals/data/full_run/texts/EO_10859.txt), headed Executive Order 10859, signed by Dwight D. Eisenhower on February 5, 1960. The census register gives the same number, date and subject (Revocation of Executive Order 10758 Establishing a Career Executive Program Within the Civil Service System, and Executive Order 10777, Amending Executive Order 10758). The text is an official scan read through its machine text layer; I read it for OCR damage and note below where damage matters. Inventory: the order has one operative sentence, the revocation of Executive Order No. 10758 of March 4, 1958, which established a career executive program within the civil-service system, and Executive Order No. 10777 of August 6, 1958, which amended it to increase the membership of the Career Executive Board. The single sentence revokes two orders at once; I keep them in one clause because both are revoked by the same words on the same day. The order states no effective date, so it took effect when signed on February 5, 1960; the Federal Register printed it on February 9, 1960, which is the alternative date a reader might take for effectiveness. The revocation is a single act that the order performs by its own words when it issues; once made it commands nothing further, so the clause is exhausted by performance on the signing date. What survives is the fact that the revoked order no longer operates, which is a consequence of the act and not a continuing command of this order. The three chosen machine searches (U.S. Code through 2026-10-09, eCFR as of 2026-10-14, Office of the Federal Register disposition notes plus operative sentences of 17521 saved order texts) each state their coverage with no warning; their coverage notes were read. They search by this order's number, and none returned a hit for it.
